On Monday, US President Donald Trump appeared to rule out another major offensive against Iran, at least for now. After speaking with Qatar’s prime minister, he said Washington was maintaining the “status quo”.
In a Truth Social post, he said Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain and Kuwait favoured continuing the naval blockade and “Operation Iron Gate”. Further escalation was “quite unlikely”, he suggested, although US forces remained “locked and loaded”.
Days earlier, Trump had been considering new strikes. Now he appears to favour keeping Iran under economic and military pressure without risking another major war.
The flaw is obvious: Washington can choose to maintain a blockade. It cannot decide how long Tehran will tolerate it.
Also on Monday, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, called Washington a “desperate gambler”, denounced reports of “imaginary talks”, and demanded that the US “surrender” to Iran’s conditions.
Trump sees a manageable stalemate; Tehran sees an unacceptable siege.
For the Islamic Republic, this confrontation is existential. An indefinite blockade would inflict mounting economic damage, without guaranteeing relief or protection from another attack. Meanwhile, Gulf producers continue selling whatever oil they can export. Iran is left bleeding while others continue business.

Analysis: The changing face of Israel’s ultra-Orthodox politics
ne of the most significant developments in the aftermath of the Israeli elections was the decision by United Torah Judaism (UTJ), the main ultra-Orthodox Jewish party, not to recommend Benjamin Netanyahu to form the next government.
This marks a departure from years of close alliance between Netanyahu and the ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, parties, long considered a pillar of Israeli politics.
Even if the move was tactical, intended to strengthen the Haredi parties’ bargaining position, it sends an important signal, as last month’s vote exposed several significant shifts within Haredi society.
They include the declining standing of veteran political leaders, a struggle over the future of Haredi leadership, the emergence of a new political force challenging established conventions from within, and a deepening crisis surrounding the model of the “society of learners”.
The trauma of the Hamas-led 7 October attack may have bypassed the Haredi spiritual leadership and its veteran MPs, but the wider Haredi public, including the generally more conservative Lithuanian community, understands that something momentous has happened in Israel. This is particularly true of the younger generation.

One of the most significant developments in the aftermath of the Israeli elections was the decision by United Torah Judaism (UTJ), the main ultra-Orthodox Jewish party, not to recommend Benjamin Netanyahu to form the next government.
This marks a departure from years of close alliance between Netanyahu and the ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, parties, long considered a pillar of Israeli politics.
Even if the move was tactical, intended to strengthen the Haredi parties’ bargaining position, it sends an important signal, as last month’s vote exposed several significant shifts within Haredi society.
They include the declining standing of veteran political leaders, a struggle over the future of Haredi leadership, the emergence of a new political force challenging established conventions from within, and a deepening crisis surrounding the model of the “society of learners”.
This social model developed in Israel, where Torah study in yeshivas and kollelim has become a central way of life and even a social ideal for Haredi men. Many devote years to religious study instead of entering the labour market or undertaking military service.
The model rests on the belief that Torah study is a supreme value and a communal obligation, supported financially by families, the community, the state and religious support networks.
For decades, the Haredi parties were among the most stable and predictable blocs in Israeli politics. One of the world’s leading scholars of Ottoman history, Engin Deniz Akarli, died in his home in Istanbul on Sunday, aged 81.
Professor Akarli’s research focused on the legal, political and economic history of the late Ottoman Empire, as well as the Middle East. His scholarship engaged deeply with neglected areas of research in these fields.
One of his most influential works, The Long Peace: Ottoman Lebanon, 1861-1920 (University of California Press, 1993) challenged Eurocentric narratives on state-building and governance that centre western intervention through a close study of the Mount Lebanon Mutassarifiya (governorate) following the civil war of 1860.
He demonstrated that Lebanese self-rule, institutions and local religious reconciliation in this period laid the foundations for secular democracy that was hampered by European intervention.
Born in the northwestern Turkish city of Eskisehir, Professor Akarli completed his primary and secondary education at Eskisehir Maarif College, and graduated from the Department of Business Administration and Economics at the prestigious Robert College (now Bogazici University), in 1968.
He continued his education in the United States, first at Wisconsin University for his Master’s studies, and then at Princeton for his PhD.
His teaching career spanned several universities multiple continents. After completing his doctoral studies, he returned to Turkey as one of the founding professors of the history department at Bogazici University.

Iran defends two-day proposal for peace talks after US rejects conditions
Iran defended a proposal on Monday to restart peace talks in as few as two days as the most reasonable offer on the table, after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called some of Iran's conditions "outrageous and ridiculous".
"Is it unreasonable that Iran demands that US illegal sanctions and its naval blockade must be lifted before negotiations start and that the war should end on all fronts?" Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told a weekly press conference in response to Rubio's remarks.
Iran has made the offer to shorten the time to restart talks from an earlier seven-day proposal, which calls for Washington to first meet conditions including halting hostilities, lifting a blockade and waiving sanctions.
Baghaei also said US pressure on Iraq to close most of its borders with Iran should not affect bilateral ties with Baghdad, after Iraq's foreign minister said Washington was pushing for such a move. Baghaei dismissed a US military task force aimed at restricting Iran's land trade as a diversion following President Donald Trump's Republicans' losses in midterm elections.
Reporting by Reuters

A sand embankment collapsed on tents sheltering displaced Palestinians in the Gaza Strip late on Sunday, killing three children and two women as severe weather battered the territory.
At least five other people were rescued with injuries by Civil Defence search-and-rescue teams at the makeshift camp in Deir al-Balah, where operations to locate missing people continued.
Mahmoud Basal, spokesperson for the Palestinian Civil Defence in Gaza, said the massive sandy embankment and surrounding mounds of earth collapsed after a low-pressure weather system brought torrential rain and strong winds to the Strip over the weekend.
Two of those killed were identified as Mariam Nabhan and her son, Salah Nabhan. The other three were Reem al-Zain, Habiba al-Zain and Ibrahim al-Zain.
Weekend downpours flooded an estimated 70,000 temporary tents sheltering displaced families across Gaza, leaving thousands of people exposed to the elements.
Palestinians have blamed Israel’s genocide and ongoing siege for the worsening conditions facing displaced people.
“This is not simply the result of severe weather. It is the direct consequence of prolonged Israeli genocide, the widespread destruction of infrastructure, continued displacement, and the denial of essential humanitarian assistance and adequate shelter,” the Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Saturday.
The ministry said nearly two million Palestinians were living in approximately 270,000 tents across Gaza in “appalling humanitarian conditions”.

Meanwhile, Al Jazeera reports that Israel deported 14 western activists who were attempting to protect Palestinians as they harvested their olives. The Human Rights Defenders Fund said the group were arrested on Friday near Ramallah after being atacked by Israeli settlers.
October has seen an unprecedented surge in Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians attempting gather the olive harvest compared to previous years. OCHA documented 377 olive-harvest-related settler attacks across the West Bank between September 1 and November 2, 2026, outstripping the total recorded during a any previous olive harvest season.

A witness told Reuters that they saw blown-out windows across several floors of the Aramco Tower, one of the tallest buildings in the capital's King Abdullah Financial District.

Aramco was not immediately available for comment, and there was no immediate statement from the Houthis.
Multiple loud booms were heard in Riyadh earlier on Sunday, a Reuters witness said, shortly after Saudi Civil Defense issued an early-warning alert of a potential threat in the region. Authorities later announced that the danger had passed.
